stories.title: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant & Bar Inks Deal at 63 Cooper Square
stories.excerpt: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant & Bar is opening its fourth location in New York City and its fifth overall, Commercial Observer has learned. The growing Northern Chinese dining concept signed a 2,000-square-foot lease at 63 Cooper Square, an East Village property owned by Matthew Rettner, according to landlord broker Meridian Capital Group. Asking rent for the space was $21,600 per month, and the tenant signed a 15-year lease. The midblock site is one of several small commercial spots on the ground floor of a residential building along Third Avenue between St. Marks Place and East Seventh Street. “Cooper Square doesn’t have a ton of turnover, so when a turnkey restaurant space becomes available there, we want a tenant who can hit the ground running,” Meridian’s Daniel Zacaim said in a statement. “Dongbei’s operating history made this an easy recommendation to the landlord, and I think this location is going to perform very well for them.” Zacaim represented the landlord alongside Noam Aziz and Carson Shahrabani, while David Green and Benjamin Namdar of KSR negotiated on behalf of the tenant. The KSR brokers did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “What’s impressive about Dongbei is the consistency of their growth — four locations in New York plus a New Jersey expansion in the works,” Shahrabani said in a statement. “That kind of momentum makes landlords comfortable, and it made this negotiation move quickly and smoothly on both sides.” Dongbei has Manhattan locations at 953 Columbus Avenue on the Upper West Side, 367 West 36th Street in Midtown and 17 Ann Street in the Financial District, as well as a spot in Downtown Jersey City. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant signs 2,000 sq ft lease at 63 Cooper Square, East Village Manhattan.
15-year lease at $21,600/month ($129.60/sq ft annually) signals ground-floor retail confidence.
Restaurant chain expanding to fourth NYC location reflects discretionary spending and foot traffic recovery.
stories.summary: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant & Bar leased 2,000 square feet at 63 Cooper Square in Manhattan's East Village on a 15-year term at $21,600 per month ($129.60/sf/yr). This is the growing Northern Chinese concept's fourth NYC location and fifth overall. The deal demonstrates landlord confidence in tenant operator quality and signals retail leasing activity in a tight ground-floor market with low turnover.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. Ground-floor retail leasing in East Village does reflect modest demand recovery and foot traffic confidence, which can support mixed-use development feasibility, but this single tenancy is insufficient to shift broader market signals. Monitor if retail recovery accelerates in Manhattan submarkets where residential development is planned.

stories.title: Power Is No Longer an Input in Data Centers. It Is the Product.
stories.excerpt: A data center site can have land, fiber, approvals and a customer ready to deploy, and still be nearly worthless. The reason is changing what developers are actually searching for. Power scarcity is changing the economics of development. On power grid operator PJM, capacity prices jumped from $28.92 per megawatt-day for 2024-2025 to $269.92 for 2025-2026, then climbed again to $329.17 for 2026-2027. Power availability is increasingly becoming the asset around which everything else is assembled. Suhail Y Tayeb. PHOTO: Courtesy NYU Land and fiber still matter. But neither creates a viable project if electricity cannot arrive when the customer needs it. That changes the site-selection conversation. Where is the substation? How much capacity is actually available? When can the first tranche of power be delivered? A hyperscaler may ultimately need hundreds of megawatts, but not all on day one. If 50 megawatts can be energized now and another 100 can arrive 18 months later, that site may be more valuable than one promising 300 megawatts several years from now. Power is not valuable simply because it exists on a utility map. It is valuable when it can be delivered. That distinction is forcing developers deeper into the energy business. They are pursuing utility relationships, transmission access, substations and gas infrastructure with the same intensity they once reserved for land and entitlements. They are also confronting a mismatch in timelines. AI companies plan deployments in months. Major transmission projects, substations and generation assets can take much longer. The result is a growing market for solutions that bridge the gap. Behind-the-meter generation, co-generation and direct energy partnerships are increasingly part of the conversation. The question is no longer simply whether a utility can serve a project, but whether and how the developer can assemble an energy system until the grid catches up. bullets: PJM power capacity prices surge: $28.92/MW-day (2024-25) to $329.17/MW-day (2026-27).
Power availability, not land or fiber, now primary site-selection constraint for data center development.
Phased power delivery (50 MW now, 100 MW in 18 months) outweighs promised future capacity.
stories.summary: Power grid capacity costs on PJM have exploded from $28.92 per megawatt-day in 2024-25 to $329.17 in 2026-27. Electricity delivery timing and availability have become the primary constraint for data center projects, superseding land and fiber availability. Developers now prioritize sites where power can be energized immediately in tranches rather than projects promising large future capacity.
stories.impact: Severe constraint on data center supply pipeline across PJM footprint (Northeast, Mid-Atlantic, Midwest). Power scarcity will slow new hyperscaler facilities and redirect capital away from regions without grid capacity, potentially concentrating demand in other regions (Southwest, Texas). For multifamily developers, this slows job creation in data center hubs and may reduce population in-migration to markets reliant on data center employment growth. Monitor Texas, Arizona, and other low-cost power regions for competing capital flows.

stories.title: Anthony Cohen of Northmarq: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s Anthony Cohen is six years into his commercial real estate career and already holds top roles at a firm noted for its leasing, sales and debt acumen. Cohen, 34, is a managing director in Northmarq’s Los Angeles commercial investment sales office and co-leader of the firm’s national net-lease and sale-leaseback group. Since 2020 — when he started his real estate brokerage career at Ascension — Cohen has worked on deals with a cumulative volume exceeding $1 billion. His experience in both real estate and finance — he worked at J.P. Morgan for two years after college — make him a pro at advising businesses on their real estate needs. Cohen, who leads a team of five producers at Northmarq, said the most popular investment today is one that saves buyers money on taxes: accelerated depreciated assets like gas stations, car washes or even oil change sites. “Those are the most interesting and most highly sought-after assets right now,” he said. Commercial Observer sat down with Cohen last week to discuss that investment trend, his career so far, and what he’s seeing in the market today. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: Walk me through how you got started in real estate and where you were before Northmarq. Anthony Cohen: So I’m not too young, but not too old. I went to Penn State. I studied finance. My first job was at J.P. Morgan. I was working just outside of Philadelphia in Delaware, actually, and I was a financial analyst there, and, you know, did really well. Even though I got all the accolades of being a high performer, it’s very corporate, and upward mobility compensation is very hard to change. You just have to put in the hours and the years, and you’ll eventually be moving up the ladder. It was a really good experience to learn how to become a professional in the outside world, but I wanted something that had unlimited potential. bullets: Northmarq MD Anthony Cohen reports $1B+ deal volume in 6-year career, primarily net-lease and sale-leaseback.
Accelerated depreciation assets (gas stations, car washes, oil change sites) most sought-after investment class.
Tax-driven buyer demand reshaping commercial investment preference hierarchy.

Cohen has completed over $1 billion in deal volume in his first six years in CRE.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Reflects capital allocation trends in non-residential real estate but does not signal shift in multifamily fundamentals, financing, or development economics. Note: Tax policy sensitivity among commercial investors may influence GAFO (general merchandise) retail and support services demand in mixed-use projects, but this is secondary.

stories.title: Sunday Summary: Sharp Left
stories.excerpt: Summer’s done, and the hustle of fall will soon be upon us. Part of the background noise of the season will be the elections for state and federal legislatures. That includes the New York State Senate and Assembly. Those august Albany chambers are about to absorb a relatively large number of Democratic Socialists — and their allies — in the same vein as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. That could have serious ramifications for commercial real estate. We’re talking retail rent control; further restrictions on raising the rent on, or vacating, rent-stabilized apartments; and a much longer moratorium on the development of large-scale data centers. There’s also some potential good news in so many far-left pols heading up the Hudson at once: They have aggressive plans for fostering the development of much-needed affordable housing. Those plans should align with the commercial real estate industry’s own efforts (really). Otherwise, though, next year could bring regressive changes akin to the dreaded 2019 state housing legislation that followed lefty wins in the 2018 elections. Options can be a lifesaver Speaking of affordable housing, a niche financing option for the asset class is growing in popularity. It’s called tax-exempt commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) debt. That debt can carry lower costs of capital than standard taxable CMBS or the affordable housing loans that Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac back. (For more on the state of CMBS, check out our Q&A with Trepp’s Stephen Buschbom and Andy Boettcher.) And, apropos of both legislatures and affordable housing, there’s a lot to recommend for the CRE industry in the recently enacted 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. It’s the biggest single piece of federal housing legislation in decades, and it’s meant to foster a lot of new housing construction, particularly of the subsidized sort. Will it? bullets: Democratic Socialists and left-leaning allies gaining seats in NY State Senate and Assembly this fall.
Proposed policies: retail rent control, stricter rent-stabilized restrictions, data center moratorium, affordable housing initiatives.
Regulatory risk to commercial real estate offset by potential affordable housing subsidy opportunities.
stories.summary: New York State legislative elections will bring a wave of Democratic Socialists and their allies to Albany, potentially enacting policies including retail rent control, tighter rent-stabilized apartment restrictions, extended data center moratoriums, and aggressive affordable housing development mandates. This represents a significant political shift that could reshape commercial real estate regulation.
stories.impact: HIGH IMPACT on New York multifamily and mixed-use development. Stricter rent regulation and rent-stabilized tenant protections increase operating cost and regulatory risk for market-rate and value-add operators; reduced development feasibility in regulated submarkets. Conversely, aggressive affordable housing subsidies and tax incentives may open capital for below-market-rate development and public-private partnerships. Data center moratorium will constrain job growth and population in-migration in upstate markets (Tech Valley) but may redirect talent and capital back to downstate NYC. Remodel underwriting assumptions for NY markets and monitor PILOT/TIF availability for affordable projects.

stories.title: Global Holdings Lands $382M Refi for Midtown Tower
stories.excerpt: Private equity firm Global Holdings has secured a $382.4 million refinancing loan for its Midtown Manhattan office tower at 120 Park Ave., with Wells Fargo and German bank LBBW originating the note. The funding, reported by The Real Deal, retires the property’s existing $335 million loan from HSBC. The recapitalization follows Bloomberg LP’s renewal in late 2025 of its 495,753-square-foot lease across 20 floors of the Class A building, marking one of the city’s largest lease deals of the year. Bloomberg’s lease, which was extended to 2024, accounts for roughly 80% of the property’s rentable area. Global Holdings acquired the 620,000-square-foot building neighboring Grand Central Terminal from Altria Group in 2008. The refinancing will facilitate a capital improvement program for the asset, which was built in 1981. Chaired by Eyal Ofer, Global Holdings has an international real estate portfolio spanning more than 10 million square feet of real estate, including 120 properties and over 1,500 hotel rooms. The post Global Holdings Lands $382M Refi for Midtown Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Global Holdings refi $382.4M for 120 Park Ave., Midtown Manhattan (Wells Fargo, LBBW), up from $335M prior.
Bloomberg LP renewed 495,753 sq ft lease (20 floors, ~80% of building) in late 2025 to 2034.
Deal follows capital improvement program, signals Class A office stability despite broader office headwinds.
stories.summary: Global Holdings secured a $382.4 million refinancing from Wells Fargo and LBBW for its 620,000-square-foot Class A office tower at 120 Park Ave. in Midtown Manhattan, replacing a $335 million HSBC loan. Bloomberg LP's renewal of 495,753 square feet (20 floors, ~80% of rentable area) to 2034 underpinned the refinancing and capital improvement program for the 1981-built asset.
stories.impact: Modest positive signal for Midtown Manhattan office market; Bloomberg's long-term commitment suggests high-credit-quality tenants still value trophy Class A space near Grand Central and transit. However, limited macro relevance to multifamily development. Office refi activity does not materially affect residential supply, demand, or cost. Note: large office renewals reduce urban office vacancy, which can support retail and foodservice tenants that complement mixed-use residential projects, but this is indirect.

stories.title: NYC Plans 215-Unit Bronx Apartment Building
stories.excerpt: New York City’s Department of Housing Preservation & Development (HPD) has filed plans for a 215-unit apartment building on a vacant city-owned lot in the Bronx’s Melrose neighborhood. The 176,000-square-foot building at 3116–3124 Third Ave. would rise 20 stories, the New York Business Journal reported, citing plans filed with the New York City Planning Commission. HPD revealed that it has chosen Bronx-based developer Procida Cos. and community development nonprofit Nos Quedamos for the project. The building would also come with 7,000 square feet of commercial space and amenities including a community room, second-floor terrace and roof terrace. If realized, the project would advance the Melrose Commons Urban Renewal Plan, which proposes to bring new affordable housing across a 33-block area. To make way for the project, HPD is requesting that the city remove the 85-foot height limit for new multifamily developments in the vicinity. The department has also asked the Planning Commission create an Urban Development Action Area Program within the neighborhood that would set forth guidelines for developing income-restricted and affordable housing. The post NYC Plans 215-Unit Bronx Apartment Building appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NYC HPD plans 215-unit, 20-story building at 3116-3124 Third Ave., Melrose, Bronx (Procida Cos., Nos Quedamos).
City seeks height limit waiver (85 ft → taller) and Urban Development Action Area Program for 33-block Melrose Commons.
Project advances public affordable housing push; 7,000 sf retail + community amenities included.
stories.summary: NYC's Department of Housing Preservation & Development filed plans for a 215-unit, 176,000-square-foot, 20-story apartment building in Melrose, Bronx, in partnership with developer Procida Cos. and nonprofit Nos Quedamos. The project includes 7,000 square feet of ground-floor retail and community facilities. HPD is requesting a height limit waiver and Urban Development Action Area Program designation to advance the 33-block Melrose Commons Urban Renewal Plan.
stories.impact: MODERATE POSITIVE DEMAND SIGNAL for Bronx multifamily development. Public sector investment in affordable housing and land assembly (removal of height restrictions) reduces regulatory friction and signals committed demand for Melrose neighborhood. Zoning relief sets precedent for private developers in the 33-block area, improving project feasibility and reducing entitlement costs. However, project targets affordable (income-restricted) rather than market-rate units, limiting rent upside for private operators. Monitor if zoning relief accelerates private market-rate and mixed-income development in surrounding blocks; third-party development should benefit from improved zoning and community infrastructure.

stories.title: Northern New Jersey Shopping Center Changes Hands
stories.excerpt: Adoni Property Group has acquired the 60,614-square-foot shopping center in Northern New Jersey’s Basking Ridge from Kushner Real Estate Group. JLL Capital Markets arranged the sale and secured $12.2 million in acquisition financing on behalf of the buyer through an unidentified life insurance firm. Built in 2000, the community retail center spans approximately 11 acres at 546 Allen Rd. and includes five buildings that were fully leased to 18 tenants at the time of the sale. Four new leases executed within the past 12 months point to continued momentum at the property. Anchored by Walgreens and United States Postal Service locations, the shopping center sits within the master-planned community The Hills at Basking Ridge. “Highlands Village is a premier, necessity-based retail center with a proven history of stability and long-term tenant loyalty,” said Sonny Adoni, founder and CEO of Adoni Property Group in a statement. Westfield, NJ-based Adoni develops and manages a diversified portfolio of residential and commercial properties. Headquartered in Jersey City, Kushner Real Estate Group is a real estate investment and management firm with a portfolio of apartments and commercial space across four states. The post Northern New Jersey Shopping Center Changes Hands appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Adoni Property Group acquires 60,614 sq ft shopping center in Basking Ridge, NJ from Kushner RE for $12.2M debt.
Fully leased (18 tenants) with anchors Walgreens, USPS; 4 new leases in past 12 months.
Master-planned community retail shows stability; necessary-based retail remains resilient.
stories.summary: Adoni Property Group acquired a fully leased 60,614-square-foot community retail shopping center in Basking Ridge, Northern New Jersey, from Kushner Real Estate Group. The 11-acre property at 546 Allen Rd., built in 2000, includes five buildings anchored by Walgreens and USPS, with 18 total tenants. Four new leases in the prior 12 months and $12.2 million in acquisition financing reflect continued tenant demand.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Retail center acquisition signals stable necessary-based retail fundamentals in suburban New Jersey (Basking Ridge is affluent, master-planned community). This can support mixed-use development in nearby markets, but does not drive residential demand or supply shifts. Note: master-planned community health is positive signal for multifamily feasibility in the submarket if residential component is planned.

stories.title: Iconic Rancho Cordova Furniture Showroom Listed for Sale
stories.excerpt: The longtime Rancho Cordova showroom of Beck’s Furniture has been listed for sale. The 208,800-square-foot property at 11840 Folsom Blvd has served primarily as a warehouse and distribution center for Beck’s Furniture, where people came to view the chairs and sofas before buying. The company closed its doors last year. The 10 acres along the Highway 50 corridor and has served as one of Northern California’s most recognizable furniture destinations for nearly 50 years. It features an approximately 90,000 square feet of showroom space and 120,000 square feet of warehouse and distribution space. Morrow Botros, Bryce MacDonald and Jay Hamer of Cushman & Wakefield have been exclusively retained to market the asset on behalf of the seller, Beck’s Furniture & Sleep / Beckinger Family Ownership.  Botros added, “For nearly 50 years, the Beck’s Furniture campus has stood as one of the Sacramento region’s most recognizable commercial landmarks. Few properties can claim both institutional scale and deep community recognition.” The post Iconic Rancho Cordova Furniture Showroom Listed for Sale appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Beck's Furniture flagship showroom, 208,800 sq ft in Rancho Cordova, CA listed for sale after 50-year run.
Property features 90,000 sq ft showroom + 120,000 sq ft warehouse on 10 acres along Highway 50 corridor.
Company closure signals legacy retail consolidation; large, single-use warehouse space faces repositioning risk.
stories.summary: The iconic Beck's Furniture showroom and distribution center in Rancho Cordova, California, a 208,800-square-foot, 10-acre asset (90,000 sf showroom, 120,000 sf warehouse) along the Highway 50 corridor, has been listed for sale. Beck's closed operations last year after nearly 50 years as a regional furniture landmark. Cushman & Wakefield is marketing the asset.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development in multifamily-focused markets. However, signals legacy retail vacancy in secondary markets (Sacramento region). Potential adaptive reuse opportunity if site is rezoned for mixed-use or industrial; large format warehouses in suburban locations may be repurposed for logistics or light industrial, which could indirectly support employment in the region. Monitor if Sacramento multifamily developers consider mixed-use redevelopment of similar large-footprint retail sites; zoning and entitlement case study.

stories.title: Tishman Speyer Trades Mountain View Office Building for $121.5M
stories.excerpt: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street, a 100 percent leased, Class A office building in downtown Mountain View, California. Spear Street Capital was the buyer in the $121.5 million transaction. Tishman Speyer developed the 138,000-square-foot property in 2002 and immediately leased the office space in full to Fenwick & West, which has remained a customer in the building. Tishman Speyer claims the transaction represents one of the strongest pricing outcomes for a Mountain View office sale in recent years. Centrally located with convenient access to highways and Caltrain, 400 Castro features expansive roof decks, underground parking and views of the San Francisco Bay and coastal mountains. The property, which was 100% leased at the time of the sale, is located in the heart of Downtown Mountain View, surrounded by restaurants and retail, with Cascal restaurant, Peet’s Coffee, and Sweetgreen on site. Tishman Speyer was represented by the Eastdil Secured team led by Nate Jones. The post Tishman Speyer Trades Mountain View Office Building for $121.5M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Tishman Speyer sells 400 Castro Street, Mountain View, CA (138,000 sq ft) to Spear Street Capital for $121.5M.
100% leased to Fenwick & West (law firm tenant since 2002 delivery); Class A downtown location.
Transaction 'strong pricing outcome' for Mountain View office despite broader West Coast office challenges.
stories.summary: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street, a 138,000-square-foot, fully leased Class A office building in downtown Mountain View, California, to Spear Street Capital for $121.5 million. The building, developed in 2002, has been 100% leased to Fenwick & West law firm since delivery. Tishman Speyer noted the transaction represents one of the strongest pricing outcomes for Mountain View office sales in recent years.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. Mountain View office sale reflects continued investor appetite for fully-leased, high-credit trophy assets; does not signal broad office market recovery. However, signal that downtown Mountain View remains attractively positioned for mixed-use redevelopment (office + multifamily) due to walkability, transit (Caltrain), and employment density. For TCR teams considering California mixed-use developments, downtown Silicon Valley nodes remain defensible due to tech job concentration, though office-to-residential conversion remains challenging. Monitor if similar trophy office sales create redevelopment opportunities for adaptive reuse.

stories.title: Related Secures $65M Refi for Office Property in L.A.’s South Bay
stories.excerpt: The owners of a 301,000-square-foot Class A office property in Los Angeles’ South Bay have secured refinancing for the property. Owners Related Companies and Cruzan landed the $64.7 million loan from Waterfall Asset Management and Delaware Life for the eight-story property called the Torrance, named after its home city. The asset at 21250 Hawthorne Boulevard is 93 percent occupied, according to Yardi Matrix, with tenants including All Nippon Airways, Salon Republic, Barrister Executive Suites, Compass California, Unio Health Partners and Morgan Stanley. Newmark’s Jordan Roeschlaub, Nick Scribani and Chris Lozinak arranged the debt. The property was built in 1988. Related and Cruzan acquired it from Stream Realty Partners for $106.8 million in 2017, and secured $59.2 million in refinancing in 2022. The South Bay has benefited from surging demand from aerospace and defense users for both office and industrial space. But the Greater Los Angeles office market remains deeply bifurcated. Overall vacancy was at 25.3 percent after the second quarter, nearly unchanged from year-end 2025, while trophy properties have a 13.5 percent vacancy rate, according to Newmark research. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Related Companies and Cruzan refi 301,000 sq ft office property (The Torrance, South Bay LA) for $64.7M.
Property 93% occupied with corporate tenants (ANA, Morgan Stanley, health/salons); built 1988.
South Bay benefiting from aerospace/defense demand for office and industrial; broader LA office market bifurcated.
stories.summary: Related Companies and Cruzan secured a $64.7 million refinancing from Waterfall Asset Management and Delaware Life for The Torrance, a 301,000-square-foot, eight-story Class A office building in Los Angeles' South Bay at 21250 Hawthorne Boulevard. The property is 93% occupied with tenants including All Nippon Airways, Morgan Stanley, and health services firms. The deal reflects South Bay's strength driven by aerospace and defense sector demand, though broader LA office market remains bifurcated.
stories.impact: MODERATE POSITIVE SIGNAL for South Bay LA multifamily development. Aerospace and defense industry resilience in South Bay (reflected in strong office demand and refi at 93% occupancy) drives regional employment stability and population in-migration. This supports multifamily demand and rental growth in Torrance, Hawthorne, Manhattan Beach, and El Segundo submarkets. However, bifurcated broader LA office market indicates limited spillover to weaker office nodes; multifamily development should target aerospace/defense employment centers. Monitor aerospace sector for expansion announcements (SpaceX, Northrop Grumman, Boeing South Bay operations); job growth directly translates to rental demand in South Bay multifamily.
